title: Mechanisms and functions of the transcription factor broad as a terminal selector in the fly visual system
text:
Precise development and maintenance of neuronal identity underlie all cognitive function. This proposal aims to
investigate how terminal selectors differentiate neuronal identity and subsequent wiring patterns between similar
neurons in the Drosophila (fruit fly) visual system. Identity based mechanisms discovered here may inform
strategies to overcome human neurodevelopmental and neuropsychiatric disorders that disrupt maintenance of
neuronal identity.

title: Pyk2 inhibition mitigates immunosuppressive environment and enhances therapeutic response to immune checkpoint inhibitors in GBM
text:
This project aims to improve immunotherapeutic outcomes for glioblastoma (GBM) patients by
investigating the role of Pyk2 and FAK signaling in regulating PD-L1 expression in GBM and their
impact on the tumor immune microenvironment. The study will explore the potential of Pyk2/FAK
inhibitors as sensitizers for anti-PD-L1 therapy in GBM, considering the importance of
incorporating the NF1 status of the tumor in treatment decisions. The findings will contribute to
personalized therapeutic approaches and treatment choices, with the goal of enhancing outcomes
for GBM patients.

title: Generation and analysis of mouse models to define the roles of the ALS-associated factor Zfp106/ZNF106 in neurodegeneration
text:
Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and related motor neuron diseases affect more than 30,000 people in the
United States, and 90% of ALS patients die within 5 years of diagnosis. It is well known that there is a strong
genetic component to these degenerative diseases, yet many of the genetic causes remain poorly defined. The
proposed studies will investigate the genetic functions of a gene ZNF106 newly understood to be involved in
human ALS-like neurodegeneration to determine how ZNF106 mutations cause motor neuron degeneration.

title: Microfluidic, molecular, and optical tools for multimodal measurement of single cells and tissues
text:
PROJECT NARATIVE
The development of single-cell genomics technologies has been a driving force in biomedical research over the
past decade because of the throughput, sensitivity, and precision with which such techniques can dissect
complex biological systems. The goal of this research program is to develop new hardware and software tools
for multimodal precision measurements of single cells and tissues to drive the next generation of data-driven
systems biology research.

title: Mechanisms of epithelial alterations in diabetic cornea
text:
Relevance of the proposed research project to public health
The application addresses PA-20-185 goal as a Research Project Grant on new ways of treating
stem cell and wound healing defects in diabetic corneal disease. We will focus on normalizing human
diabetic corneal epithelial stem cells through the iPSC technology, as well as through a combination
of nano and epigenetic therapy for maximum effect. If successful, the proposal may have a high
impact for future treatment of frequent wound healing-related corneal problems in diabetic patients.

title: UCSD Cancer Center Training Program in Drug Development
text:
This application seeks funding to continue a training program in developmental therapeutics focused on cancer
drugs at the Moores Cancer Center at the University of California, San Diego. Our vision is that cancer can be
controlled with novel drug, immunologic and viral therapeutics directed at molecular targets that allow
individualization of treatment. The mission of the program is to provide training to postdoctoral PhD and MD-
physician-scientists in each of the major steps in the development of novel cancer therapeutics so as to position
these individuals to play leading roles in translating laboratory-based discoveries into safe and effective
therapeutic agents.

title: Defining mechanisms of action of Menin inhibition in AML
text:
PROJECT 3
Despite significant progress in treating acute leukemia, acute myeloid leukemia (AML) continues to be a
challenging diagnosis with a poor prognosis for both adults and children, highlighting a crucial area of unmet
medical need. AML is characterized by the hijacking of normal transcriptional networks by large epigenetic
complexes that suppress normal myeloid differentiation and drive malignant transformation. Thus, we propose
an innovative strategy to target aberrant epigenetic control of gene regulation by (a) characterizing the unique
protein complexes and chromatin structures controlling leukemic gene expression and (b) targeting these multi-
subunit complexes with drug combinations and/or proteolysis targeting chimeras (PROTACs).

title: Elucidating the role of circPMS1 in melanoma metastasis.
text:
While the survival rate of early-stage melanoma is 90%, the 5-year survival of metastatic melanoma (stage III-
IV) is only 30%. The molecular mechanisms that underly melanoma metastasis are still poorly understood, in
particular the role of non-coding RNA such as circular RNAs. This proposal is focused on understanding how
circRNAs drive melanoma metastasis, which will allow us to open new avenues for targeted therapies in
melanoma treatment.

title: Local nano-immune modulation for the systemic treatment of lymphoma
text:
Despite the success of immunotherapies and cellular therapies, most aggressive lymphomas will relapse with
no consensus on the next best treatment strategy. We found recently that photothermal therapy with a toll-like
receptor 9 agonists coated branched gold nanoparticle in a murine lymphoma model had (1) improved local and
systemic anti-lymphoma T cell responses, (2) increased mature dendritic cells populations in lymph nodes, and
(3) increased memory T cells populations in the spleen and untreated tumors. In this proposal, we will first further
characterize the immune response of our photothermal therapy platform in various B cell lymphoma models,
then combine our platform with T cell engaging immunotherapies such as checkpoint inhibitors and bispecific
antibodies, and lastly examine a subcutaneous lymphoma lysate/nanoparticle mixture photothermal therapy
platform for patients without easily accessible diseased lymph nodes.

title: Impact of HIV-1 5' Leader Defects on plasma viremia, proviral dynamics, and immune responses
text:
Despite effective therapy, HIV infection remains an incurable chronic disease. Defective proviruses that continue
to express viral RNA and proteins contribute to persistent viremia and chronic immune activation. Aligned with
NIH’s goals to understand HIV persistence and reduce the burden of lifelong treatment, this project will define
the mechanisms by which proviruses with 5’ Leader defects evade immune clearance, characterize their
contribution to viremia, and investigate their impact on HIV-specific immune responses. By developing a novel
assay to detect 5’ leader defects and integrating single-cell and immunologic profiling, this work will provide
people with HIV and their care providers with improved tools to monitor infection, and inform new strategies to
target the HIV reservoir.

title: CLEC7A in microglia biology and Alzheimer's disease
text:
In recent years, the C-type lectin receptor CLEC7A has emerged as a widely used marker of disease-associated
microglia in Alzheimer’s disease models; yet, the actual role of CLEC7A in neurodegenerative disease
pathogenesis has not been studied in great detail to date. In our preliminary studies, we revealed that genetic
deletion of CLEC7A in a mouse model of Alzheimer’s disease leads to greatly reduced levels of amyloid beta
deposition, increased recruitment of microglia to plaques, and significantly improved neuronal health. For this
project, we will leverage a unique combination of CLEC7A conditional knockout mouse strains, CLEC7A-
deficient human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived microglia-like cells, and CLEC7A modulating agents to
further uncover roles for CLEC7A in the regulation of microglia responses and Alzheimer’s-related disease
progression.

title: Regulation of Foamy Macrophage Differentiation and Survival in Atherosclerosis
text:
Atherosclerosis is driven by the accumulation of cholesterol in the aortic intima that deposits within “foamy”
macrophages present in plaque. We will address the mechanisms that Trem2 uses to promote foamy cell
formation through cholesterol uptake, and regulation foamy macrophage lipid metabolism and cholesterol efflux.
Finally, we will test a novel therapeutic drug that binds and triggers activation signal through Trem2 for treatment
of existing atherosclerotic plaques, knowledge that is necessary for translation of these findings into future patient
studies.

title: Safe-OPTION: Optical Physiology To Interrogate Oligonucleotide Neurotoxicity
text:
Antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) have emerged as a novel therapeutic modality for central
nervous system (CNS) disorders. However, significant challenges remain for efficient
identification of optimal ASO drug candidates which lack acute or delayed CNS toxicity in pre-
clinical species. We propose implementing a machine learning model combined with in vitro
neuronal functional assays using our all-optical electrophysiology platform to establish a
predictive platform for ASO safety evaluation across rodents and non-human primates. Adopting
this platform would significantly save ASO drug development cost, reduce animal
experimentation, and accelerate drug discovery.

title: Targeting lymph node metastases to block cancer progression
text:
Cancer draining lymph nodes are important for the generation and maintenance of anti-cancer immune
responses. However, the presence of metastatic cancer cells in these lymph nodes inhibits immune responses
and the efficacy of new therapies intended to boost anti-cancer immunity. In the proposed work, we will identify
and overcome the mechanisms of immune suppression in metastatic lymph nodes to improve therapeutic
outcomes for patients with metastatic cancer.

title: Unmasking the role of maternal transcript UTRs in reproductive fecundity
text:
While animal embryos receive approximately equal amounts of DNA from each of their parents, nearly all of
their cytoplasm is inherited from the female gamete. This cytoplasm contains information in the form of
maternal proteins and mRNAs that are used by the embryo prior to “zygotic gene activation”, the point at which
maternal mRNA is cleared and the embryo becomes reliant upon its own genome. We seek to understand how
this maternal information is stored in the cytoplasm during oogenesis, then decoded after fertilization. We use
C. elegans, a well-established genetically tractable invertebrate model organism, to study this process.

title: Cancer Model Development
text: CANCER MODEL DEVELOPMENT SHARED RESOURCE (CMD) The overall mission of The Jackson Laboratory Cancer Center (JAXCC) is to bring genomic solutions to cancer medicine. Our basic research goal is to tackle the question of “Genetics and Genomics of Aging and Cancer”, while our translational intent is to contribute new concepts, technologies, and clinical education initiatives originating from basic science to advance precision cancer medicine. The Cancer Model Development Shared Resource (CMD) supports JAX Cancer Center members in the design, development, and use of sophisticated in vitro and in vivo models of cancer. The goal of this integrated Shared Resource is to provide end-to-end model development solutions for JAXCC investigators, facilitating navigation of the various components and services required to move from concept to the utilization of specific models for their own research. Critically, the CMD leverages the wealth of models available in JAX repositories and the deep expertise and experience of CMD staff to facilitate the development and use of such models by JAXCC members who have limited experience and/or infrastructure to design and execute such genetic manipulation and/or experimentation in their own laboratories. CMD consists of four services: Genetic Engineering Technologies (GET), which provides services to engineer and produce complex, precisely tunable, genetically engineered mouse models of cancer; the Genetically Engineered Mouse Models (GEMMs) service focusing on end-to-end project consultation and management of studies involving new or existing mouse models of cancer; Xenograft and Live Imaging Services (XLIS), which supports all aspects of xenograft project planning and colony management including creation and engraftment, compound testing, generation of new xenograft models, and live imaging; and Cellular Engineering (CE), which provides high-quality, custom-edited lines of human induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs), offering a range of allele types that include knock-outs, knockins, single-base variants, and conditional loss-of-function alleles. To accomplish CMD’s goal of serving as a one-stop shop to support cancer model development and application, the Specific Aims of the CMD Shared Resource are: Aim 1: Support the creation and use of genetically engineered models for cancer research; Aim 2: Provide access to a comprehensive suite of resources and services for the construction, use, and imaging of patient-derived xenograft (PDX) mouse models; and Aim 3: Support the use of unique resources including those from the JAX Center for Aging Research (JCAR) and strain heterogeneity panels to develop improved models of cancer.

title: Deciphering Disc Degeneration: Untangling the Roles of Age and Inflammation
text:
Degeneration of intervertebral disc is closely associated with low back pain which afflicts 52 million individuals
in the United States. The outcomes of the proposed studies will provide supporting data to develop new
diagnostic tools and treatment strategies for disc degeneration.

title: Bioinformatics Shared Resource (BISR)
text: BIOINFORMATICS SHARED RESOURCE (BISR) The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center (MD Anderson) Bioinformatics Shared Resource (BISR) provides cutting-edge support in bioinformatics and computational biology for all nine research programs. BISR includes 15 faculty, 11 bioinformaticians, 1 bioanalyst, and 3 software engineers, all from the Department of Bioinformatics and Computational Biology (DBCB). BISR provides comprehensive, highly collaborative study design, analysis, modeling, and interpretation of large, complex datasets using mathematical and statistical principles and methodologies. BISR supports all types of omics technologies (e.g., spatially resolved, single-cell, functional proteomics, flow cytometry, mass spectrometry, CRISPR) using statistical, machine learning, artificial intelligence (AI) and large language model (LLM) methods. Particular points of innovative focus include data quality control and data visualization. BISR aims are to provide: 1) exceptional, cutting-edge bioinformatics support; 2) exceptional cancer-focused academic endeavors for research support continuity; 3) new computational tools for biomedical researchers; 4) top-quality training for specialists and non-specialists; and 5) support for career development for faculty, trainees, and others. DBCB, a leader in bioinformatics nationally and internationally, provides high-quality academic research, education, and computer science as vital infrastructure for BISR functions. BISR benefits from an institutionally supported high-performance computing environment with a >1500-core cluster, 140 virtual servers, and 2.5 petabytes of storage. Support for research projects can be requested through 1) the BISR website, 2) weekly “walk-in” Zoom clinics, 3) informal contact, or 4) a BISR faculty liaison assigned to each department or program. There is no charge-back for services, but users are expected to provide support for effort through grants on large projects. During 2024, BISR supported 110 members (88% of user base) with peer-reviewed funding from all nine RPs. This includes support for MD Anderson’s currently funded and recently concluded Specialized Programs of Research Excellence (SPORE) grants and reflects the critical importance of BISR services to Cancer Center Support Grant (CCSG) members. In 2024, BISR supported 129 publications, with 54% in high-impact journals (Impact Factor ≥10), while this represents a decrease in total publications when compared to 2019, the quality has substantially increased as noted by the increase of high IF publications. Future plans include: 1) development of top interactive computational tools and resources, based on Next-Gen Clustered Heat Maps and MBatch (used to date in > 60 NCI projects); 2) accelerated pursuit of Aims 1 to 5, including support of peer-reviewed grants, publications, and programs; 3) increased expertise and application of AI/LLM expertise; and 4) increased bioinformatician continuing-education. The combination of expert BISR PIs and dedicated BISR bioinformaticians provides reliable, cutting-edge support.

title: Digital Mobile Technologies to study Tuberculosis: A Multi-disciplinary Program
text: Tuberculosis disease affects more than 10 million people and kills at 1.3 million people across all countries each year. The observed rates are disproportionately higher in among the low- and middle-income countries including Uganda. In the U.S major disparities in cases of tuberculosis disease and deaths persist in subgroups of its population. In 2024, more than 12,300 cases of tuberculosis were reported in the U.S which represents an 8% increase compared to the previous year. The current proposal is built upon the premise that digital mobile technologies can be utilized innovatively as tools to provide useful information in the prevention and control of tuberculosis transmission, infection, and disease. The proposed training program will build research capacity of a critical number of interdisciplinary scientists with diverse backgrounds such as epidemiology, public health, geography, mathematics and computer science to enable them to apply new technologies and analytic methods to study an old disease like tuberculosis. We will apply advanced machine learning and artificial intelligence across the training program. This novel approach to cross-disciplinary training will advance the research agenda of the U.S and Uganda as a partner country.

title: From protein structures to effective drugs via machine learning and molecular simulation
text:
The proposed research focuses on development of computational methods to tackle long-
standing problems critical to the efficient design of safe, effective drugs: given the folded structure
of a protein, how does one design chemical compounds that bind to that protein tightly and
specifically, and how does one design compounds that have the desired effect on the protein’s
function? This research will enable the development of novel therapeutics to reduce illness and
disability, supporting the NIH’s mission.
